title: T22 Position Sizing and Risk Budget

lines.text: Lesson twenty-two: position sizing and risk budget. Size a position from the risk you accept.
lines.say: Lesson twenty-two: position sizing and risk budget. Size a position from the risk you accept.

lines.text: Two traders, one fictional chart. Both buy BTC at 60,000, with a stop-loss at 59,400.
lines.say: Two traders, one fictional chart. Both buy B-T-C at sixty thousand, with a stop-loss at fifty-nine thousand four hundred.

lines.text: Trader A's position is worth 500 USDT. Trader B's is worth 10,000 USDT.
lines.say: Trader A's position is worth five hundred U-S-D-T. Trader B's is worth ten thousand U-S-D-T.

lines.text: Price falls to the stop. A loses 5 USDT. B loses 100 USDT. Same stop, very different damage.
lines.say: Price falls to the stop. A loses five U-S-D-T. B loses one hundred U-S-D-T. Same stop, very different damage.

lines.text: Your account balance is the money in your trading account. Here, a 1,000 USDT practice account.
lines.say: Your account balance is the money in your trading account. Here, a one thousand U-S-D-T practice account.

lines.text: Your risk budget is the most you accept to lose on one trade, decided before you enter.
lines.say: Your risk budget is the most you accept to lose on one trade, decided before you enter.

lines.text: Like deciding how much you'll spend at a fair before you go, not halfway through.
lines.say: Like deciding how much you'll spend at a fair before you go, not halfway through.

lines.text: In this example the budget is 10 USDT. An example only, not a recommendation.
lines.say: In this example the budget is ten U-S-D-T. An example only, not a recommendation.

lines.text: Stop distance is the gap between your entry price and your stop-loss price.
lines.say: Stop distance is the gap between your entry price and your stop-loss price.

lines.text: Entry 60,000, stop 59,400: the distance is 600 USDT. As a share of entry, 600 ÷ 60,000 = 1%.
lines.say: Entry sixty thousand, stop fifty-nine thousand four hundred: the distance is six hundred U-S-D-T. As a share of entry, six hundred divided by sixty thousand equals one percent.

lines.text: For a short, the stop sits above entry. Entry 60,000, stop 60,300: 300 USDT, or 0.5%.
lines.say: For a short, the stop sits above entry. Entry sixty thousand, stop sixty thousand three hundred: three hundred U-S-D-T, or zero point five percent.

lines.text: Position size is how much of the coin you hold. Notional is what it's worth: size × price.
lines.say: Position size is how much of the coin you hold. Notional is what it's worth: size times price.

lines.text: 0.01 BTC at 60,000 USDT is a notional of 600 USDT.
lines.say: Zero point zero one B-T-C at sixty thousand U-S-D-T is a notional of six hundred U-S-D-T.

lines.text: If price falls 1% to the stop, you lose 1% of the notional: 600 × 1% = 6 USDT.
lines.say: If price falls one percent to the stop, you lose one percent of the notional: six hundred times one percent equals six U-S-D-T.

lines.text: Like buying rice: if the price per kilo drops, ten kilos lose ten times more than one.
lines.say: Like buying rice: if the price per kilo drops, ten kilos lose ten times more than one.

lines.text: Turn it around to find the allowed notional.
lines.say: Turn it around to find the allowed notional.

lines.text: Allowed notional ≈ risk amount ÷ stop distance as a share of entry.
lines.say: Allowed notional about risk amount divided by stop distance as a share of entry.
Ten divided by (six hundred divided by sixty thousand) equals ten divided by zero point zero one equals one thousand U-S-D-T. That's about zero point zero one six seven B-T-C at sixty thousand.

lines.text: For the short, with a 0.5% stop: 10 ÷ 0.005 = 2,000 USDT.
lines.say: For the short, with a zero point five percent stop: ten divided by zero point zero zero five equals two thousand U-S-D-T.

lines.text: This simple model ignores fees, slippage, contract rules and liquidation.
lines.say: This simple model ignores fees, slippage, contract rules and liquidation.

lines.text: Leverage lets a small margin control a bigger notional. Leverage = notional ÷ margin.
lines.say: Leverage lets a small margin control a bigger notional. Leverage equals notional divided by margin.

lines.text: A 1,000 USDT notional needs 500 margin at 2x, 200 at 5x, 100 at 10x.
lines.say: A one thousand U-S-D-T notional needs five hundred margin at two ex, two hundred at five ex, one hundred at ten ex.

lines.text: But the loss at the stop is still about 10 USDT. It depends on notional and stop distance.
lines.say: But the loss at the stop is still about ten U-S-D-T. It depends on notional and stop distance.

lines.text: High leverage makes huge positions easy to open, and brings liquidation closer.
lines.say: High leverage makes huge positions easy to open, and brings liquidation closer.

lines.text: Drawdown is how far your account falls from its highest point, shown in %.
lines.say: Drawdown is how far your account falls from its highest point, shown in percent.

lines.text: Five 10 USDT losses take 1,000 down to 950. A 5% drawdown.
lines.say: Five ten U-S-D-T losses take one thousand down to nine hundred fifty. A five percent drawdown.

lines.text: Five 100 USDT losses take it to 500. A 50% drawdown.
lines.say: Five one hundred U-S-D-T losses take it to five hundred. A fifty percent drawdown.

lines.text: From 500, you'd need +100% just to get back to 1,000. Small risks keep drawdowns small.
lines.say: From five hundred, you'd need plus one hundred percent just to get back to one thousand. Small risks keep drawdowns small.

lines.text: A common mistake: choosing leverage or size first, like 'I'll use 20x', then hoping.
lines.say: A common mistake: choosing leverage or size first, like 'I'll use twenty ex', then hoping.

lines.text: The fix is a fixed order: risk budget, then stop, then notional, then check the margin.
lines.say: The fix is a fixed order: risk budget, then stop, then notional, then check the margin.

lines.text: And if the allowed size is too small to make sense, NO_TRADE is a fine answer.
lines.say: And if the allowed size is too small to make sense, no trade is a fine answer.

lines.text: Your turn. Account 2,000 USDT, example budget 20 USDT. Long at 50,000, stop at 49,500.
lines.say: Your turn. Account two thousand U-S-D-T, example budget twenty U-S-D-T. Long at fifty thousand, stop at forty-nine thousand five hundred.

lines.text: What's the allowed notional? A: 200, B: 2,000, or C: 20,000 USDT? Pause and work it out.
lines.say: What's the allowed notional? A: two hundred, B: two thousand, or C: twenty thousand U-S-D-T? Pause and work it out.

lines.text: B. The stop is 500 away, which is 1%. So 20 ÷ 0.01 = 2,000 USDT.
lines.say: B. The stop is five hundred away, which is one percent. So twenty divided by zero point zero one equals two thousand U-S-D-T.

lines.text: C is tempting, but at the stop it loses 200 USDT, ten times the budget.
lines.say: C is tempting, but at the stop it loses two hundred U-S-D-T, ten times the budget.

lines.text: A calculator should warn you when inputs make no sense.
lines.say: A calculator should warn you when inputs make no sense.

lines.text: Stop equal to entry? The distance is zero, so there is no sensible size.
lines.say: Stop equal to entry? The distance is zero, so there is no sensible size.

lines.text: A long with the stop above entry? That stop is on the wrong side.
lines.say: A long with the stop above entry? That stop is on the wrong side.

lines.text: A risk budget bigger than the whole account? That's impossible.
lines.say: A risk budget bigger than the whole account? That's impossible.

lines.text: Know the limits of this maths.
lines.say: Know the limits of this maths.

lines.text: Stops can slip, and fees add to the loss. The real loss can be bigger than planned.
lines.say: Stops can slip, and fees add to the loss. The real loss can be bigger than planned.

lines.text: With high leverage, liquidation can come before your stop. Exchanges also set minimum sizes.
lines.say: With high leverage, liquidation can come before your stop. Exchanges also set minimum sizes.

lines.text: Fictional examples, not advice or recommended percentages. NO_TRADE is always allowed.
lines.say: Fictional examples, not advice or recommended percentages. No trade is always allowed.

lines.text: Let's recap.
lines.say: Let's recap.

lines.text: One: decide your risk budget before you enter. Examples here are not recommendations.
lines.say: One: decide your risk budget before you enter. Examples here are not recommendations.

lines.text: Two: allowed notional ≈ risk ÷ stop distance as a share of entry. A simple model.
lines.say: Two: allowed notional about risk divided by stop distance as a share of entry. A simple model.

lines.text: Three: leverage changes the margin, not the loss at the stop. Watch drawdown.
lines.say: Three: leverage changes the margin, not the loss at the stop. Watch drawdown.

lines.text: Check yourself: risk 10 USDT, stop 2% away. Allowed notional?
lines.say: Check yourself: risk ten U-S-D-T, stop two percent away. Allowed notional?
About five hundred U-S-D-T: ten divided by zero point zero two equals five hundred.

lines.text: Next up: T23, the full scalping decision lifecycle. From chart to journal, in a demo.
lines.say: Next up: T twenty-three, the full scalping decision lifecycle. From chart to journal, in a demo.
